title: What is alive?
source: DeepKids Combined. Covers Cambridge Stage 1 Biology Unit 1.1 'Animals and plants alive!' (living, once living and never living; animals and plants are both alive). No textbook needed.
summary: Your child sorts the world into things that are alive, things that were once alive and things that were never alive, and discovers that it's harder than it looks. A seed looks dead but is alive and sleeping; a wooden chair was once a tree; a lump of yeast wakes up and blows up a balloon. They find the signs living things show, see that plants are as alive as animals, notice that every living thing needs water, air and food, and meet a palm tree that grew from a seed 2,000 years old.
subconcepts: alive, once alive and never alive
signs living things show: growing, feeding, drinking, breathing, moving or responding, making young
plants are alive too, in a slower way
a seed is a sleeping baby plant (dormant)
waking a seed needs water and warmth (germination)
living things can die and then can't wake again
tiny living things too small to see (yeast, microbes)
once-alive materials at home: wood, cotton, paper, silk, wool, leather
all living things need water, air and food
living things make young like themselves
living things depend on non-living things (sun, water, soil, air)
humans are one kind of living thing among millions
you are a team: tiny living things live in and with you
builds_on: This is the first time. In Class 3 your child comes back to the question with the seven signs scientists use (MRS GREN), cells, harder cases (fire, crystals, viruses, robots) and the environment. In Class 5, microorganisms and how life began.
goals: By the end your child can sort things into alive, once alive and never alive, and give a reason for each.
By the end your child can name what living things do: grow, need food, water and air, breathe, move or respond, and make young.
By the end your child can show that a seed is alive even though it looks dead, by making it grow, and say what wakes it.
By the end your child can say that animals and plants are both alive, even though plants don't walk.
By the end your child can find once-alive things in their own home and say what living thing they came from.
By the end your child can ask 'how do you know?' about whether something is alive.
words: growing, needing food, water and air, and responding to the world
was part of something alive but isn't any more, like wood or a dry leaf
was never alive, like a stone, glass or steel
a baby plant sleeping inside a coat, with its packed lunch
alive but asleep and waiting, like a dry seed
when a seed wakes up and starts to grow
tiny living things, too small to see one by one, that make dough and idli batter rise
the babies of a living thing
the things a living thing must have to stay alive: water, air, food

days.title: Alive, or not?
days.goal: Sort things and argue about the tricky ones.

steps.title: The mystery bag
steps.do: Put in a bag: a stone, a seed (a rajma bean), a leaf, a wooden spoon, a toy car, an apple, a shell and a pinch of yeast in a small packet. Pull out one at a time. Your child says 'alive!', 'not alive!' or 'I'm not sure!' and why. Don't correct anything yet; just say 'Interesting! Let's find out.'

steps.title: Sort into three
steps.do: Make three circles on the floor with string or chalk: 'alive', 'once alive', 'never alive'. Sort the things. Give the hint for 'once alive': 'it was part of something alive, but isn't now' (the wooden spoon was a tree; the shell was a snail's house; the leaf fell off a tree). Leave the seed and the yeast in an 'I'm not sure' pile; this week we will test them. Then do sections A and B of Worksheet ws1 together: read each word aloud and your child taps the right box.

steps.title: How do you know?
steps.do: For each thing in 'alive', ask: 'How do you know it's alive?' Write the reasons on a big sheet as your child says them: it grows, it eats, it drinks, it breathes, it moves by itself, it has babies. Read the list back. This is your 'signs of life' sheet; stick it on the wall for the week. Ask: 'Do you show these signs?' (Yes! You grow, eat, drink, breathe, move.) Say: 'So you are a living thing, one of millions of kinds of living things on Earth.'

need: a bag with a stone, a rajma bean, a leaf, a wooden spoon, a toy car, an apple, a shell, a packet of yeast

days.title: Is a seed alive?
days.goal: Test the 'not sure' pile: can a seed wake up?

steps.title: Seed detectives
steps.do: Look closely at a dry rajma bean with a hand lens. Ask: 'Does it breathe? Move? Eat? Grow?' Most children say no. Ask: 'So is it alive?' Write down your child's answer on the signs sheet with today's date, so you can check it later.

steps.title: Wake the seeds
steps.do: Do Experiment e1: soaked beans on damp cotton, dry beans on dry cotton, and beans a grown-up has boiled, on damp cotton. Ask your child to predict first and draw the three cups. Say the new word: 'A seed that is alive but asleep is called dormant. When it wakes up and grows, we say it germinates.'

steps.title: Dance: wake like a seed
steps.do: Your child curls up tight on the floor like a dry seed: still, quiet, 'asleep'. You are the rain: sprinkle your fingers over them and say 'water... warmth...'. Very slowly they push out one foot (the root, going down), then an arm (the shoot, going up), then uncurl and stretch tall like a seedling reaching for the Sun. Ask: 'When you were curled up, were you alive?' (Yes, just asleep.)

steps.title: Story: The Seed That Slept for Two Thousand Years
steps.do: Read the story aloud (Story tab). Then ask the 'Talk about it' questions. Listen especially for: 'The baby palm was inside the seed all along' and 'The water woke it up.'

need: a hand lens if you have one
a few beans boiled by a grown-up

prep.task: Soak 3 beans in water overnight; boil 3 more for 10 minutes and let them cool

days.title: Plants are alive too
days.goal: Find living things and their signs outdoors, and see that plants are alive.

steps.title: Seed check
steps.do: Look at the three seed cups. Are the soaked beans fatter? Has a skin split? Your child draws what they see. Keep cup A and cup C damp.

steps.title: Living things hunt
steps.do: Go outside for 15 minutes with the hunt list in Worksheet ws2: something growing, something breathing, something eating, something moving by itself, something with babies or eggs, something once alive, something never alive. Lift a stone gently to look for minibeasts, then put it back exactly as it was. Look at ants carrying food, a bird pecking, a pigeon's nest (look, never touch), moss on a wall, a new leaf on a plant. Your child ticks or draws on the clipboard.

steps.title: Is a tree alive?
steps.do: Stand by a tree or a pot plant. Ask: 'Is it alive? It doesn't walk or eat food like us.' Go through the signs sheet: does it grow? (Yes: new leaves, it gets taller.) Drink? (Its roots drink water from the soil.) Eat? (It makes its own food in its green leaves, using sunlight.) Breathe? (Through tiny holes in its leaves.) Move? (Slowly: leaves turn towards the light, flowers open and close.) Make young? (Seeds.) Say: 'Plants and animals are both alive. Plants just do it more slowly and quietly.' Ask: 'What would a tree say about how fast we rush around?'

days.title: Tiny life wakes up
days.goal: See that some living things are too small to see.

steps.title: Seed check and the cloth-seller
steps.do: Look at the seed cups and draw them. Then tell your child about voice v2: a cloth-seller with no degree who made his own tiny glass lenses and was the first person to see living things too small for our eyes. Ask its question.

steps.title: The balloon that blows itself up
steps.do: Do Experiment e2 with yeast, sugar, warm water and a balloon. While you wait, ask: 'Yeast looks like brown sand. Is sand alive? What would yeast need to do to show us it is alive?' (Grow, eat, breathe, make more.) When the balloon fills, say: 'Yeast is millions of tiny living things. They were dormant, like the seeds. Warm water and sugar woke them up, they ate, and they breathed out a gas.' Move yeast from 'not sure' to 'alive'.

steps.title: Alive or Not? card game
steps.do: Play the card game (g1): sort cards into alive, once alive and never alive, and argue about the tricky ones. Every time someone places a card, the others may say 'How do you know?'

days.title: Once alive, all around the house
days.goal: Find things in the home that were once part of living things.

steps.title: Seed check
steps.do: Look at the seed cups. Often a white root has come out of the soaked seeds by now. Ask: 'Which way is the root going?' (Down.) 'Have the boiled seeds done anything?' (No.) Draw it.

steps.title: Once-alive treasure hunt
steps.do: Do Activity a1, the once-alive treasure hunt. Your child finds 10 things in the house that were once part of something alive and, for each, says which living thing it came from: a wooden chair (a tree), a cotton kurta (a cotton plant), a newspaper (trees), a silk dupatta (silkworms), a woollen shawl (sheep or goats), a leather belt (a cow or goat), a jute bag (a jute plant), a coconut shell, honey (made by bees from flowers), rice and dal (plants). Ask: 'Is most of our food once alive?' (Yes, nearly all of it, except salt and water.)

steps.title: Babies like their parents
steps.do: Name a mother and your child names the baby: cow–calf, hen–chick, dog–puppy, cat–kitten, goat–kid, frog–tadpole, butterfly–caterpillar, human–baby. Ask: 'Does a mango seed grow into a coconut tree?' (No, a mango tree.) 'Does a stone have babies? Does a toy?' Say: 'Living things make young like themselves. Never-alive things can't.' Do section C of Worksheet ws1.

need: a basket for the treasure hunt

days.title: What every living thing needs
days.goal: See that living things need water, air and food, and depend on non-living things.

steps.title: The boiled seeds
steps.do: Look at the seed cups. The soaked seeds have roots and maybe a shoot; the dry seeds haven't changed (they are still asleep); the boiled seeds never grew. Ask gently: 'Why didn't the boiled seeds grow?' (Boiling killed the baby plant inside. Living things can die, and then they can't wake up again. That's why we look after living things carefully.) Now put the dry seeds on damp cotton too, and watch them wake up tomorrow.

steps.title: Needs, not wants
steps.do: Ask: 'What do you need to stay alive?' Help your child sort ideas into needs (water, air, food, a safe place, sleep) and wants (a toy, TV, sweets). Then ask the same for a crow, a tulsi plant and the yeast: crow (water, air, food, a tree to nest in), plant (water, air, sunlight, soil), yeast (water, warmth, sugar). Say: 'Every living thing needs water, air and food. And look: water, air, sunlight and soil are not alive. Living things need non-living things to live.' Draw a big tree in the middle of a page, and your child draws arrows from the sun, a cloud, the air and the soil to it. Finish with a surprise: 'Tiny living things live in you too: about as many bacteria live in and on your body as there are cells of you, and many help you digest food. And deep inside every cell of yours are tiny power-makers that were once free-living bacteria, long, long ago. A scientist called Lynn Margulis was laughed at for saying so, and she turned out to be right. So you are not just one living thing: you are a team.'

steps.title: Voice v1 and the project
steps.do: Talk about voice v1: a scientist named Elaine Solowey woke up a seed that had slept for 2,000 years, after her friend Sarah Sallon asked the question others laughed at. Ask its question. Then start the project: your child puts a tray on the table, divides it into three with paper strips, and begins to collect things for the 'alive museum' (a seedling from the cups, a feather, a shell, a stone, a coin).

need: small things from home and garden

days.title: The museum opens
days.goal: Show what you know and wonder about the hard cases.

steps.title: Finish the museum
steps.do: Finish the project tray: alive, once alive and never alive, 3–5 things each. Your child says (and you write) a label for each: 'Feather. Once alive. It came from a pigeon.' Put a sprouting seed from the cups in the 'alive' section.

steps.title: Hard cases
steps.do: Do Worksheet ws3 together, reading each question aloud and writing your child's words. Then ask the big questions: 'Is fire alive? It eats wood, grows, moves and needs air.' 'Is the Sun alive?' 'Is a cloud alive?' There's no wrong answer; ask 'How could we find out?' each time. Say: 'Scientists still argue about some tricky cases. You'll meet them again in Class 3.'

steps.title: Museum tour and teach it back
steps.do: Your child is the museum guide for the family, explaining each section and how they know. Visitors ask the check questions. Finish with your child teaching back: 'How can you tell if something is alive?' and 'Was the dry seed alive?'

Draw or write what you found outside.

How does a plant move?

sections.p: How does a plant get its food?

A pigeon is sitting on eggs on a ledge. Which sign of life is that?

experiments.title: Wake the seeds
experiments.question: Is a dry seed alive?
need: 3 beans boiled for 10 minutes by a grown-up
steps: Cup A: the 3 soaked beans on damp cotton.
Cup B: 3 dry beans on dry cotton.
Cup C: the 3 boiled beans on damp cotton.
Keep A and C damp. Look every day for a week and draw.
On Day 6, move the dry beans onto damp cotton and watch them wake too.
experiments.observe: Which cups sprout; the white root pushing out and turning down; the boiled beans going soft and never sprouting.
experiments.why: A seed is a baby plant, alive but resting (dormant), with stored food. Water and warmth wake it up and it germinates, using its stored food to grow a root and shoot. Dry seeds stay asleep until they get water; boiling kills the baby plant inside, so it can never grow.
experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the beans and lets them cool.

experiments.title: The balloon that blows itself up
experiments.question: Can something too tiny to see be alive?
need: half a cup of warm (not hot) water
steps: Put the yeast and sugar in the bottle.
Pour in the warm water and swirl.
Stretch the balloon over the neck of the bottle.
experiments.predict: Ask: 'What will happen to the balloon?'
experiments.observe: The bubbles in the bottle and the balloon slowly filling.
experiments.why: Yeast is made of millions of tiny living things (a kind of fungus). Dry yeast is asleep; warm water wakes it up, and it eats the sugar and breathes out a gas (carbon dioxide) that fills the balloon. That's also why idli batter and bread dough rise.
experiments.safety: Use warm, not hot, water. Don't drink the mixture.

activities.title: Once-alive treasure hunt
steps: Your child walks round the house with a basket and collects (or names) 10 things that were once part of a living thing.
For each, they say which living thing it came from: tree, cotton plant, sheep, silkworm, bee, cow, coconut palm, rice plant.
Lay them in a row with a paper label: 'from a tree', 'from a sheep'.
Count: how many came from plants? How many from animals?
Look round the room: is anything never alive? (glass, steel, stone, plastic)
activities.outcome: A row of once-alive things and the surprise that much of a home, and nearly all our food, was once alive.

project.title: My alive museum
steps: Find a tray and divide it into three sections with paper strips.
Collect 3–5 things for each: alive (a seedling from the seed cups, a small pot plant), once alive (a feather, a shell, a dry leaf, a wooden peg), never alive (a stone, a coin, a plastic toy).
Write (or dictate) a label for each saying how you know.
Give the family a museum tour.
project.outcome: A small museum and a child who can explain each object.

game.title: Alive or Not?
rules: Cut out the cards. Put the three heading cards (yellow) on the table.
Take turns picking a card and putting it under the right heading, saying why.
Others can challenge: 'I don't agree, because…'
Some cards are tricky on purpose. If you can't agree, make a fourth pile: 'We're not sure!'

cards.back: never alive (but made from oil, which came from ancient living things!)

big: How can a seed be alive if it doesn't move or eat?
Is a robot alive if it can move and talk?
Plastic is made from oil, and oil came from creatures that lived millions of years ago. So was plastic once alive?
Is a person more important than an ant, or a tree? Who decides?
If tiny living things live inside you and help you, are you one living thing or many?

challenge.q: People say living things are things that move. Is that right?
challenge.hint: A tree doesn't walk, and a dry seed doesn't move at all, but they're alive. A toy car moves but isn't. Moving isn't enough, and it isn't needed either.

challenge.q: Is it easy to tell what's alive?
challenge.hint: Scientists still argue about it! Some say viruses are alive, some say they're not. Even NASA had to write down a definition to know what to look for on other planets.

challenge.q: We call some plants 'weeds'. Are they less alive than the plants we grow?
challenge.hint: A weed is just a plant growing where a person doesn't want it. It grows, drinks, makes food and makes seeds like any other plant. The word tells you about us, not about the plant.

perspectives.view: For a seed, waiting is part of being alive. It can wait years for the right rain. Ask: what are you good at waiting for?

Many communities in India and around the world treat rivers, hills and forests as living beings to be respected, and in 2017 a law in New Zealand gave the Whanganui River the rights of a legal person. Ask: is a river alive? Why might people say so?
Earthworms eat dead leaves and turn them into soil that plants need. To a worm, a fallen leaf isn't rubbish, it's dinner. Ask: what would the garden be like with no worms?

Margulis argued that the energy-makers inside our cells (mitochondria) were once free bacteria that came to live inside bigger cells. Fifteen journals turned her paper down before one printed it in 1967; DNA evidence later showed she was right. Ask: if parts of you were once other living things, where do 'you' begin and end?

voices.who: Elaine Solowey and Sarah Sallon, Israel (2005)
voices.idea: Sarah Sallon obtained ancient date-palm seeds found at the old desert fortress of Masada. Elaine Solowey, a plant scientist, soaked them, fed them and planted them. One sprouted. Scientists dated a piece of its shell to about 2,000 years old. They named the tree Methuselah.
voices.then: Many people thought a seed that old must be dead. It became the oldest seed ever known to grow.
voices.now: Methuselah is now a tall palm that has made pollen, and the team has woken more ancient seeds. Seeds can sleep, alive, for centuries.
voices.ask: The seed was alive the whole 2,000 years, just asleep. Can something be alive and look completely dead? What else might be like that?

voices.idea: Van Leeuwenhoek sold cloth for a living and never went to university. He taught himself to grind tiny, powerful lenses, and in the 1670s he saw, in a drop of pond water and in scrapings from his own teeth, swarms of tiny moving creatures he called 'animalcules'.
voices.then: When he wrote to the Royal Society in London, the learned men there doubted him. They sent people to check, and eventually saw the creatures too.
voices.now: He was right: he was the first person to see bacteria and other microbes, tiny living things that are everywhere, including the yeast in our balloon.
voices.ask: The experts doubted a cloth-seller with no degree. Why do you think they didn't believe him at first? How did he prove it?

story.title: The Seed That Slept for Two Thousand Years
text: Long, long ago, on a high, hot hill in the desert, there was a great fortress, and in the fortress grew a date palm. Its dates were sweet and golden, and the people who lived there ate them and dropped the seeds, and some of the seeds fell into the cracks between the stones.
One small brown seed fell into a dark, dry crack and lay very still.

Inside its hard brown coat, the seed was alive. Curled up tight was a tiny baby palm, with a packed lunch of food beside it. But it was too dry to grow, so the seed did what seeds do. It slept. It didn't eat. It hardly breathed. It waited for rain.
But no rain came into that crack. Instead, there was a terrible war at the fortress, and then the people left, and the fortress was empty, and the wind blew sand over the stones.

A hundred years went by. Then five hundred. Kings and queens were born and died all over the world. People invented books, and clocks, and ships that sailed around the Earth. The seed slept on in the dark, holding its tiny baby palm and its packed lunch, waiting.
One thousand years. Two thousand years. People invented trains, and aeroplanes, and phones.

Then one day, archaeologists came to the old fortress. They brushed away the sand very gently, looking for clues about the people who had lived there. And in a crack between the stones, they found some old, brown date seeds. They put them in a little box, and the box sat on a shelf for many more years.
Then a woman called Sarah, who studied plants as medicines, asked a question that nobody had asked before. "What if they're still alive?"
People laughed a little. Two thousand years! Surely the seeds were dead.
But Sarah took three seeds to her friend Elaine, who had a gift for growing difficult plants in the desert. Elaine looked at the old brown seeds in her palm. "Let's see," she said.

She soaked them in warm water, the first water they had tasted in two thousand years. She gave them a little food for plants. She planted them in fresh soil, and she waited, and she watered, and she waited.
Deep inside one of the seeds, something stirred. The water had found its way in. The baby palm, curled up for so long, felt it, and woke, and began to eat its packed lunch, and stretched.
Eight weeks later, Elaine went to look at the pot. A small green shoot had pushed up through the soil.
She called Sarah. They stood together and looked at it: a baby palm tree, two thousand years old and only a few weeks old, both at the same time.
They named it Methuselah, after the oldest man in an old story. Today Methuselah is taller than a grown-up, with long green leaves that rustle in the desert wind.
And somewhere, in cracks and jars and quiet dark places all over the world, other seeds are sleeping, and waiting, and alive.
story.epiphany: A seed is alive even when it shows no signs of life: it is dormant, holding a baby plant and stored food, and water and warmth wake it (germination). Living things can be alive and look dead. The turn is the shoot pushing up after 2,000 years. Underneath: two women scientists who asked the question others laughed at, and the deep patience of life (based on the true story of Methuselah, germinated in 2005).
ask: What was inside the seed the whole time?
Why didn't the seed grow in the crack?
Why did people laugh at Sarah's question? Were they right?
What does it mean to be alive and asleep?

ideas.more: Wood, cotton, paper, silk, wool, leather and shells were once part of living things. Look around: much of a house, and nearly all our food, was once alive.
Seeds, yeast and even some tiny animals can stay alive for years without eating, waiting for water.

ideas.idea: Plants and animals are both alive, and all life needs non-living things.
ideas.more: Animals eat food and move about; plants make their own food and move slowly towards light. Both grow, breathe and make young, and both need water, air and sunlight, which are not alive.

unknowns: How long can a seed sleep and still wake up? The oldest we know is about 2,000 years; nobody knows the limit.
What exactly makes something alive? Scientists still argue, especially about viruses.
How many kinds of living things are there on Earth? Nobody knows; most tiny ones have never been named.

books.title: A Seed Is Sleepy
books.author: Dianna Hutts Aston
books.why: Exactly this idea: seeds rest, wait and wake.

books.title: What's Alive?
books.author: Kathleen Weidner Zoehfeld
books.why: A Let's-Read-and-Find-Out book that compares living and non-living things simply and well.

books.title: Living Sunlight: How Plants Bring the Earth to Life
books.author: Molly Bang and Penny Chisholm
books.why: The Sun tells the story of how its light becomes plants, food and every living thing, including us. Pure oneness.

check.q: Name something alive, something once alive and something never alive.
check.a: e.g. a cat, a wooden spoon, a stone.
Grow, need food, water and air, breathe, move or respond, and make young.

check.q: Is a dry seed alive? How do we know?
check.a: Yes, it was dormant (asleep); when we gave it water, it germinated and grew.

check.q: Why did the balloon fill up?
check.a: The yeast is alive; it ate the sugar and breathed out gas.

check.q: Is a tree alive even though it can't walk?
check.a: Yes; it grows, drinks, makes food, breathes and makes seeds.

check.q: Name two things in your house that were once alive, and what they came from.
check.a: e.g. a cotton shirt from a cotton plant, a wooden door from a tree.

check.q: What do all living things need?
check.a: Water, air and food (plants make theirs using sunlight).
